citation.title: A Geometric-Enhanced Neural Network Method for Scalable and High-Resolution Topology Optimization
citation.authors: Lei Zhang, Shiqiang Li, Zhichu Lei, Guangzhe Du, Xiao Zhang, Guanbin Chen, Wenliang Qian
citation.version_coded: Version of record (MDPI open access full text)

claim.primary_outcome_paraphrase: On cantilever and Michell beam cases, GeNN reduces the checkerboard index versus unfiltered SIMP by 65.3% and 27.6%, respectively.
claim.claimed_speedup_basis: A secondary speed comparison in Section 4.3 reports SIMP at 61.36 s and GeNN at 32.55 s for the simply supported beam: 61.36 / 32.55 = 1.89. The 3D table separately implies 727.91 / 91.42 = 7.96.
claim.alternatives: Section 4.3: SS-beam compliance objective is 112,737.99 for GeNN versus 115,819.95 for SIMP, with 32.55 s versus 61.36 s; 3D cantilever results are also reported. The abstract qualitatively claims improved computational efficiency and reports a bridge case completed in under ten minutes.

baseline.implementation: Standard SIMP implementation with density filter (2D filter radius 1.3 elements; 3D 1.5 elements); code details not stated
baseline.solver: 3D linear system uses sparse direct PARDISO; 2D solver not stated
baseline.problem_size: SS beam comparison: 160 × 80 Q4 elements; 3D cantilever: 80 × 40 × 4 hexahedral elements; default 2D examples: 80 × 40 elements
baseline.ml_time: SS beam: 32.55 s; 3D cantilever: 91.42 s (Tables 1–2). High-resolution forward pass: <0.02 s; total with training about 30 s (Section 4.2).
baseline.training_time: About 30 s including training for the high-resolution inference example (Section 4.2); separate timing for the main optimization cases not stated
baseline.data_generation_cost: not applicable to per-problem optimization; no offline data-generation cost stated
baseline.quality_metric: Compliance objective value, checkerboard index, and volume fraction
baseline.quality_gap: SS beam: GeNN objective 112,737.99 versus SIMP 115,819.95 (Table 1); volume fraction set to 0.4 (Section 4).

R1.evidence: Section 4.1, Figure 7: the primary comparison is checkerboard-index quality; the protocol's speed-matching rule does not apply to this quality-only primary outcome.

R2.evidence: Section 4.1, Figure 7: the primary outcome is design quality, not a speed comparison. Later speed results are secondary.

R3.evidence: Sections 3–4: design parameters are optimized for each problem through iterative FEA and backpropagation; there is no offline training-data generation phase for this method.

R4.evidence: Sections 3–4: compliance is evaluated through FEA and volume fraction is constrained, but infeasible or failed-design rates are not reported.

reporting.n_test_cases: Multiple examples: cantilever and Michell beams, L-bracket, simply supported beam, 3D cantilever, heat conduction, multi-volume design, and bridge (Sections 4–5).

notes: The primary quantitative comparison under the protocol ordering is checkerboard-index quality in Section 4.1. The later direct classical speed comparison is recorded as an alternative outcome and in the baseline fields.
